title: Praising and criticising
subtitle: on the ball, streets ahead, pick holes in
summary: Praise people with idioms like on the ball and streets ahead, and criticise them with run down and pick holes in.

lesson.heading: The verb praise
lesson.text: You **praise** someone **for** something. **Highly praised** is a very common collocation. Note the preposition: it is never 'praise someone about something'.

examples.text: The teacher **praised** the children **for** their hard work.
examples.wrong: praised the children about their hard work

examples.text: William's acting in this film has been **highly praised**.
She plays the guitar **brilliantly**, just like her father.
He's the very best, a really **first-rate** administrator.

lesson.heading: Idioms that praise a skill
rows: good at establishing good relations with them, or at motivating them
good at talking; a fluent, confident speaker

lesson.heading: Praising idioms in sentences
lesson.text: Notice the verb each idiom takes: you **are** on the ball, but you **have** a way with people, green fingers or the gift of the gab.

examples.text: When it comes to grammar, she's really **on the ball**.
Ben **has a way with** foreign students. The other teachers envy him.
Emma really **has green fingers**; look at those flowers!
Let him do the talking; he's got **the gift of the gab**.

lesson.heading: Saying someone or something is far better

left.label: Of people
left.text: **head and shoulders above** and **miles better than** are normally used about people.
examples: Imogen is **head and shoulders above** the rest of the girls at maths.
She's **miles better than** the other girls at maths.
As far as sport is concerned, Sam is **among the best** in his class.

right.label: Of things and countries
right.text: **streets ahead of** compares organisations or countries; **out of this world** describes a thing.
examples: When it comes to technology, Japan is **streets ahead of** most other countries.
That meal was just **out of this world**.
The hotel we were staying in was **out of this world**.

lesson.note: among the best can be reversed: among the worst, among the most interesting, and so on.

lesson.heading: criticise and critical
lesson.text: **Criticise** usually means say that someone or something is bad. But it can also simply mean give an opinion or judgement about a book or film - good as well as bad.

examples.text: Paige's parents are always **criticising** her appearance.
I belong to a writers' group - we read and **criticise** each other's work.
examples.note: = give our opinion, positive and negative

lesson.heading: Four meanings of critical
rows: 1 not pleased; saying something is bad or wrong
The report is **highly critical of** safety standards at the factory.
The President's support is **critical to** this project. / a **critical** decision
3 giving opinions on books, plays, films
His last film received **critical acclaim**, meaning the critics praised it.
Both drivers are **in a critical condition** after the crash - they might die.
lesson.note: The adverb critically works with all four: critically important (2), critically acclaimed (3), critically ill or critically injured (4).

lesson.heading: Idioms that criticise
rows: say bad things about them: You shouldn't **run down** your own country when you're abroad.
find fault with every detail: Why do you always have to **pick holes in** everything I say?
be in the wrong: You are undoubtedly **to blame** and you should apologise.
be ridiculous: I think Antonio's being totally **absurd**.

lesson.heading: Criticising people
lesson.text: Four more colourful criticisms. **The cat's whiskers** and **the bee's knees** both describe someone with far too high an opinion of themselves.

examples.note: the bee's knees means exactly the same

examples.text: When it comes to time-keeping, he's **the world's worst**.
Jack is so rude. He really **takes the biscuit**.
examples.note: = is a striking example of some negative quality

examples.text: Jo wants to **have her cake and eat it**!
examples.note: = wants everything, with no contribution from her side

exercises.prompt: Match each idiom with its meaning.

pairs.left: have the gift of the gab

pairs.right: be good at getting on with people
have far too high an opinion of yourself
be a striking example of something bad

exercises.prompt: The hotel we were staying in was absolutely superb. The hotel we were staying in was ___.
exercises.explanation: Out of this world = outstanding, superb. It is usually used of things.

exercises.prompt: Giovanni is a long way above the other kids at hard sums. Giovanni is ___ the other kids at hard sums.
exercises.explanation: Head and shoulders above = far better than. It is usually used of people.

exercises.prompt: You're a long way ahead of me in understanding all this new technology. You're ___ me.
exercises.explanation: Be streets ahead of = be far more advanced than.

exercises.prompt: Maria is very good with young children - they always love her. Maria ___ young children.
exercises.explanation: Have a way with people = be good at establishing good relations with them.

exercises.prompt: Agata is a very fluent and confident speaker. Agata has ___.
exercises.explanation: Have the gift of the gab = be good at talking.

exercises.prompt: Tanya always understands a new idea immediately. Tanya is usually ___.
exercises.explanation: Be on the ball = be quick to understand.

exercises.prompt: Katya wants to buy a new car but keep all her savings too. Unfortunately, you can't ___.
options: have your cake and eat it
exercises.explanation: Have your cake and eat it = want everything, with no contribution from your side.

exercises.prompt: Is each expression praise or criticism?

exercises.statement: If someone is critically injured, their injury is only minor.
exercises.explanation: It is serious. Critically injured means so badly hurt that they might die.

exercises.statement: If a father is critical of his son's behaviour, he disapproves of it.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Be critical of = say that someone or something is bad or wrong.

exercises.statement: If your teacher asks you to criticise a film, she only wants the negative points.
exercises.explanation: No - she wants your opinion of it, good and bad. Criticise can simply mean give a judgement.

exercises.prompt: If it is 'critically important' that you finish the work by Friday, how flexible is the deadline?
exercises.explanation: Critically important means of the greatest importance, so the deadline cannot move.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order. Say the opposite of 'He often says how wonderful his school is.'
exercises.answer: He often runs down his school
exercises.explanation: Run down = say bad things about someone or something.

exercises.prompt: Say the opposite of 'Greta was not responsible for the error.' Greta was ___ for the error in the accounting figures.
exercises.hint: (two or three words with blame or fault)
exercises.explanation: Be to blame / be at fault = be in the wrong.
